justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent market price or index level near 58.1, with the 1-day estimate essentially anchoring to the last observed value given the short horizon. The slight upward slope across horizons — from 58.1 to 58.3 at one week, and 58.75 at one month — reflects a mild bullish bias, likely informed by prevailing trend momentum, mean-reversion tendencies, or a modest expected drift built into the underlying asset or index. At short horizons, the dominant driver is simply persistence: today's price is the best single predictor of tomorrow's price, so the 1-day estimate barely moves. As the horizon extends, any fundamental view about direction begins to matter more, hence the slight upward tilt.

The confidence interval widths scale predictably with time, which is consistent with how uncertainty compounds as a random walk unfolds. The 1-day interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus 0.65 from the point estimate, reflecting that over a single trading session, large moves are possible but unusual in the absence of a major catalyst. At one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 2.8, capturing the accumulated uncertainty of five trading days. By one month, the interval spans about 5.75 in each direction, reflecting the realistic range of outcomes over roughly 20 trading days when volatility, macro shifts, and sentiment changes can all compound.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro data — such as a worse-than-expected inflation print, central bank surprise, or geopolitical shock — could produce a sharp move well below the lower bound of even the monthly interval. Liquidity events, credit stress, or an unexpected earnings or policy announcement could also generate gap moves that a normally distributed model would underweight. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot, stronger-than-expected economic data, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices well above the upper bound of the monthly range.

Finally, model risk itself is a source of concern. My intervals assume something close to normal returns and relatively stable volatility, neither of which holds perfectly in practice. Fat tails in financial returns mean extreme outcomes are more probable than a Gaussian framework implies, so the true probability of being outside my 90% confidence intervals is likely somewhat higher than 10%. If realized volatility were to spike — as it does during risk-off episodes — even the 1-day interval could prove too narrow.
